## How the edit reaches the index

An issue title edit runs through the Server Action `updateIssueAction` in `src/actions/issues/update-issue.ts`. That action is built with `withAction` (`src/actions/_lib/with-action.ts`), which first parses the raw input against `updateIssueSchema`, resolves the caller into an `Actor` (via `getActor`/`requireActorFor`), and only then invokes the handler. The handler does its own permission check with `can(actor, "issue:update", …)` from `src/lib/permissions.ts`, throwing `ForbiddenActionError` if it fails, then calls `updateIssue(actor, input)` in `src/server/services/issue-service.ts`.

`updateIssue` is where the actual write happens:
1. `assertOrgScope(actor, input.orgId)` (`src/lib/tenant.ts`) — the caller's org must match the target org.
2. It re-reads the current row with `issueRepo.findIssueById`, runs `assertCan(actor, "issue:update", issueResource(before))` (a second, resource-scoped permission check with ownership escalation) and `assertNotArchived`.
3. `issueRepo.updateIssue(input)` performs the row update in the `issues` table.
4. It calls `emit("issue.updated", { …actorEnvelope(actor), issueId, projectId, changedFields })` from `src/lib/event-bus.ts`.

`emit()` looks up every subscriber registered for `"issue.updated"` and awaits them all via `Promise.allSettled` — so `updateIssue` (and therefore the Server Action) does not return until the index write has actually completed. This is why a colleague finds the new title "moments later": there's no queue or background worker in the normal path, it's a synchronous in-process fan-out within the same request.

The subscriber that matters here lives in `src/server/services/search-service.ts`, inside `registerSearchListeners()`. It's attached once at process start: `src/instrumentation.ts` calls `registerEventHandlers()` in `src/server/services/event-registry.ts`, which calls `registerSearchListeners()` alongside the activity, usage, webhook and notification listeners. The `"issue.updated"` handler deliberately ignores the event payload's fields and re-reads the row via `issueRepo.findIssueById(payload.orgId, payload.issueId)` — a comment in the file explains this is so a partially-applied write can never be indexed as if it fully succeeded — then calls `indexIssue(orgId, issue)`.

`indexIssue` (same file) builds the searchable text as `[issue.title, issue.description ?? ""].join("\n")` and calls `searchRepo.upsertSearchDocument(orgId, "issue", issue.id, content, issue.projectId)` in `src/server/repositories/search-repository.ts`. That function upserts keyed by `(orgId, subjectKind, subjectId)` rather than by row id — a comment notes the indexer is invoked on every write and must be idempotent — either updating `content`/`projectId`/`indexedAt` on the existing `search_index` row or inserting a new one.

## What's stored in the searchable copy

The target is the `search_index` table, defined in `src/server/db/schema/webhooks.ts` (`searchIndex`, lines 54–70): `id`, the tenant columns (`orgId`), `subjectKind` (`issue`/`comment`/`project`), `subjectId`, a nullable `projectId`, `content` (the raw concatenated text — for issues, title + newline + description, no tokenization or stemming), and `indexedAt`. It's a denormalized plain-text blob per document, not a real search engine — the repository's own comment calls it "a convenience layer."

There's also a background path, `runSearchReindexJob` in `src/server/jobs/search-reindex-job.ts`, which walks an org's projects/issues/comments and re-upserts everything via the same `indexIssue`/`indexComment`/`indexProject` functions. That's a drift-repair/bulk-import backstop, not part of the normal edit-to-searchable-copy flow, and it's fed by a `"search.reindex_requested"` event that `registerSearchListeners()` also subscribes to.

## What a query goes through

The colleague's search hits either the Server Action `searchAction` (`src/actions/search/search.ts`) or the JSON route `GET /api/search` (`src/app/api/search/route.ts`) used by the command palette — the route's comment notes the gating is deliberately duplicated so neither entry point is the lenient one. Both resolve an `Actor`, check `can(actor, "org:read", …)`, load the org via `getOrganizationSummary`, build a flag context with `buildFlagContext`, and narrow `kinds` to `["issue"]` unless the `advanced_search` flag is enabled (checked with `isEnabled` from `src/lib/feature-flags.ts`). The route additionally requires the `command_palette` flag. Both then call `search(actor, input)` in `src/server/services/search-service.ts`.

`search()` runs, in order:
1. `assertOrgScope(actor, input.orgId)` — tenant check.
2. `assertCan(actor, "issue:read", orgResource(input.orgId))` — permission check.
3. `consumeRateLimit(input.orgId, "search:query")` from `src/lib/rate-limit.ts` — a token-bucket keyed by `(orgId, "search:query")`, capacity scaled by the org's plan via `getPlanLimits`.
4. Loads the org and evaluates `isEnabled("advanced_search", …)` again (independently of the caller's own flag check).
5. **The refusal case**: if `input.q` contains a `:` and `advanced_search` is not enabled for that org/plan, it throws `"Field-scoped search is not included in this plan"` — a perfectly well-formed, permitted query is rejected purely because of its syntax (`status:done`-style field scoping) versus the caller's plan.
6. Only after all of that does it call `searchRepo.searchDocuments(input)`, which does a tenant-scoped `LIKE %q%` substring match against `search_index.content`, optionally filtered by `subjectKind`/`projectId`, ordered by `indexedAt`/`id` for keyset pagination (`_paging.ts`).
7. Results are mapped back to `SearchHit` (kind, id, first line of content as `title`, a snippet computed by `snippetAround`, and an `href` from `hrefFor`).

So a query can be refused at several distinct points even when it's syntactically valid and the user is properly authenticated: a tenant-scope mismatch (`TenantScopeError`), an `issue:read`/`org:read` permission failure, exceeding the `search:query` rate-limit bucket, the `command_palette` flag being off (route only), or — the subtlest case — using field-scoped (`key:value`) syntax on a plan that doesn't include `advanced_search`, which is rejected outright rather than degraded to a literal-text search.
